Hakupha
hă-kū′fah
n. (a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon)
Hebrew Chaqupha, likely connected to kaphaph, to bend or bow down, giving a sense of bent or crooked.

Biblical Definition

Hakupha names a family of Nethinim listed between two other returning households in both censuses of the return: “The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur” (Ezra 2:51), matched word for word in Nehemiah’s independent register, “The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur” (Nehemiah 7:53). Older lexicons connect the name to a Hebrew root meaning bent or bowed down, though Scripture attaches no story to the meaning; it simply preserves the family among the Nethinim, the servants given to assist the Levites in the daily work of the temple. A name that may mean bent belongs, in the record, to a household that was not broken by seventy years in Babylon — bent, perhaps, but not destroyed, and carried home again to serve at the very house of God it had been exiled from. The census frame states the outcome plainly: they “came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city” (Ezra 2:1), and were at last counted among “all Israel in their cities” (Nehemiah 7:73).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Hakupha; older lexicons connect the name to a Hebrew root meaning bent or bowed down, and it belongs to a family of Nethinim recorded identically in both Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s registers.

HAKUPHA, n. The head of a family of Nethinim, or temple servants, who returned from Babylonian captivity.

BOW, v.i. To bend the body, in token of respect, submission, or civility.

BEND, v.t. To curve, crook, or make deviate from a straight line.

SERVANT, n. A person who attends another for the purpose of performing offices for him.

NETHINIM, n. Those given; temple servants assigned to assist the Levites.

Key Scripture

Ezra 2:51 — "The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur,"

Nehemiah 7:53 — "The children of Bakbuk, the children of Hakupha, the children of Harhur,"

Ezra 2:1 — "Now these are the children of the province that went up out of the captivity, of those which had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away unto Babylon, and came again unto Jerusalem and Judah, every one unto his city;"

Nehemiah 7:73 — "So the priests, and the Levites, and the porters, and the singers, and some of the people, and the Nethinims, and all Israel, dwelt in their cities; and when the seventh month came, the children of Israel were in their cities."

Modern Corruption

A name understood to mean bent or bowed is sometimes pressed into a shame-narrative by modern popular sources eager to psychoanalyze ancient households; Scripture offers no such reading and none is warranted.

expand to see more

It has become common in casual online name-meaning sites to attach a modern emotional narrative — brokenness, low self-worth, generational trauma — to any biblical name whose root suggests bending or bowing, projecting therapeutic categories backward onto people the text never describes in those terms. The text records a household, a number, and a place in a list; it does not offer a psychological biography, and neither should its readers invent one.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that bowing, in Scripture’s own vocabulary, is most often the posture of worship rather than shame — the same body that bends before the LORD in humble service is the body He raises up. A household possibly named for bending was, in fact, restored to bow again at the house of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chaqupha, from kaphaph, to bend, bow down; shachah (H7812), to bow oneself, to worship; Nethinim (H5411), those given; golah (H1473), the exiled company.

expand to see more

Hebrew Chaqupha — likely connected to kaphaph, to bend or bow down.

Hebrew shachah (H7812) — to bow oneself, to prostrate in worship; the deeper biblical use of bending.

Hebrew Nethinim (H5411) — those given; the class of servant this household belonged to.

Hebrew golah (H1473) — the exiled company; the census is a golah-register.

Hebrew shuv (H7725) — to return; the governing verb of the whole chapter.

Usage

"“The children of Hakupha” — named identically in both Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s registers."

"“Every one unto his city” — the resettlement the whole list records."

"“The Nethinims…dwelt in their cities” — the closing summary of the return."
